title: AC calorimetric study of magneto-quantum oscillations in anisotropic multiband V$_2$Ga$_5$ superconductor
authors: Yevhen V. Petrenko, Jozef Kačmarčík, Tomáš Samuely, Jozef Haniš, Slavomír Gabáni, Szymon Królak, Michal J. Winiarski, Tomasz Klimczuk, Martin Gmitra, Peter Samuely
abstract: Unlike de Haas--van Alphen measurements, heat-capacity magneto-quantum oscillations directly probe the oscillatory bulk quasiparticle density of states. Here, we report the observation of MQOs in V$_2$Ga$_5$ single crystals studied via highly sensitive ac calorimetry. The strongest MQO signal is observed for a magnetic field applied along the vanadium chains, in excellent agreement with de Haas--van Alphen magnetization data. A single dominant frequency of 126.6 T resolved by fast Fourier transform confirms the true bulk origin of the elliptical $γ$ Fermi-surface pocket located near the Z point of the Brillouin zone. The angular dependence of the FFT frequency closely tracks the anisotropy of the $γ$ pocket, as supported by first-principles calculations. Analysis of the temperature- and field-dependent MQO amplitudes allows the precise determination of the effective cyclotron mass, Dingle temperature, quantum relaxation time, carrier mobility, and electron mean free path. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the net Berry flux is invariant with respect to the magnetic-field orientation, as a consequence of a conserved hybridization phase twist within the $γ$ pocket. These findings establish ac calorimetry as a powerful macroscopic probe of topological orbital hybridization in complex intermetallics.
summary: This work uses AC calorimetry to study magneto-quantum oscillations in the superconductor V2Ga5. By analyzing these oscillations, the authors successfully map out key parameters of the Fermi surface and demonstrate that the material exhibits a robust, field-independent Berry flux. This establishes ac calorimetry as a powerful technique for probing topological electronic hybridization in complex intermetallics.
main_problem: To probe the bulk electronic structure, including topological properties, of the superconductor V2Ga5 using heat capacity magneto-quantum oscillations (MQOs).
main_result: The study confirms a dominant Fermi surface pocket ($\gamma$ pocket) via MQO analysis and demonstrates that the net Berry flux is invariant with magnetic field orientation, establishing ac calorimetry as a powerful probe for topological orbital hybridization.
method: Highly sensitive AC calorimetry measurements of heat capacity under applied magnetic fields, analyzed using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to resolve oscillation frequencies.
model_or_system: The physical system is the single-crystalline superconductor V2Ga5. The analysis relies on Lifshitz–Kosevich theory to interpret MQO signals originating from the $\gamma$ Fermi surface pocket near the Z point of the Brillouin zone.
key_observables: Oscillation frequency (126.6 T), effective cyclotron mass, Dingle temperature, quantum relaxation time, and Berry flux ($\Phi_B$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (down to 0.3 K) and magnetic fields up to 8 T; the measured Berry phase is $\sim 0.8\pi$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that MQOs are governed by standard quantum oscillation theory, and that the observed flux invariance relates to a conserved hybridization phase twist.
figures_summary: Figures compare MQO signals in heat capacity and magnetization vs. field, show FFT spectra confirming peak frequencies (e.g., 126.6 T), and illustrate the anisotropy of the $\gamma$ pocket.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by presenting the observation of MQOs via AC calorimetry, quantifying fundamental parameters like mass and disorder ($T_D$), and culminating in a topological analysis demonstrating field-orientation invariance of the Berry flux.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the precise measurement and characterization of the geometric phase (Berry flux) using bulk thermodynamic measurements provides an experimental handle on topological electronic structure, which is relevant to advanced condensed matter theory.
